newsitem.title: USA: Analysts' U.S. corn output projections vary widely.
newsitem.headline: Analysts' U.S. corn output projections vary widely.

text.p: Slow development and widely variable corn crop conditions led to a 500-million-bushel range in analysts' U.S. corn production estimates, a Reuter survey of analysts found.

"I think clearly this is a year where we're not going to have much confidence in any of these numbers until we get the combines out," said Doug Hjort, president of Hjort Associates. "Conditions are so variable."
A Reuter survey of analysts produced an average U.S. corn production estimate of 8.857 billion bushels.
That compared with the U.S. Agriculture Department's August estimate of 8.695 billion bushels of corn. Analysts' estimates ranged from 8.555 billion to 9.085 billion bushels.
USDA will release its next estimates for this year's grain and soy production, based on conditions as of September 1, on Wednesday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.
The average analyst estimate for soybean production was 2.240 billion bushels, against USDA's August projection of 2.300 billion.

The average of analysts' estimates for U.S. wheat production was 2.268 billion bushels, including 657 million bushels of other spring wheat. USDA's August estimate was 2.249 billion bushels including 635 million of other spring wheat.

"This corn was planted late and has had some other problems," said Dave Armstrong, analyst with the Chicago Corporation who pegged U.S. corn production at 8.555 billion bushels. "I think we're not going to finish these kernels out big. I think it won't weigh up very well."
Late planting and cool summer weather slowed development in much of the U.S. Midwest.
In Iowa and Illinois, the leading U.S. corn and soybean producing states, crops were behind average development as of a week ago, the National Agricultural Statistics Service said.
But some analysts noted corn fields in Kansas and Nebraska had the potential to produce near-record yields and other areas had benefited from timely rains and warmer weather.
"I think the government was way underestimating (corn production) the last time," said Sid Love, analyst with Kropf-Love Consulting. He pegged corn production at 9.085 billion bushels.
"They were anticipating (an early) freeze and I think the crop has moved along well" since the August report, he added. "The weather hasn't really been all that bad."

Analysts' soybean projections were all below USDA's August estimate of 2.300 billion bushels. Several analysts noted USDA was unable to complete pod count surveys in time for the August report because many plants had not yet set pods.

"You're going to have a good, accurate count of the pods (on USDA's September report) but you're not going to get a good idea of how much of the pods will really be filled," said Mark Weidner, oilseeds analyst for Cargill Investor Services.
"It will still be sketchy," he added. "There's still a lot of uncertainty out there."
